Pakistan’s New Tariff on Imported Electrical Equipment Sparks Industry Concerns

KARACHI – The government’s recent imposition of a 25% tariff on imported electrical equipment, including transformers, circuit breakers, and switchgear, has sent shockwaves through Pakistan’s domestic electrical equipment industry, leading to uncertainty at manufacturing sites and among thousands of workers.

Announced last week, the policy aims to encourage local manufacturing by making imported equipment less price-competitive. However, industry experts caution that the sudden rise in import costs is having immediate impacts on ongoing operations at several major factories. “Our production processes rely on certain high-quality components which are not available locally,” said Amir Khalid, spokesperson for the Pakistan Electrical Manufacturers Association. “While the intent is to promote local industry, the abrupt increase in tariffs is disrupting our ability to meet current orders and project deadlines.”

At the Lahore facility of Jinnah Power Solutions, management reported that several assembly lines were running at reduced capacity, citing the tariff’s effect on the procurement of essential parts. “We have had to shorten shifts temporarily,” said site manager Shazia Naz, “and are in discussions with the workforce about flexible scheduling until the situation becomes clearer.”

Workers at Karachi’s National Grid Components plant voiced concerns about job security, as some shifts have already been cut and overtime suspended. “We understand the government wants to support local factories, but right now, we’re worried about our wages and future,” said technician Farhan Aziz, who has worked at the site for nine years.

Industry analysts warn that while the long-term goal may be to boost domestic capacity, the immediate disruption could impact export commitments and future investments. “Over 40% of local firms rely on imported subassemblies,” noted Uzair Siddiqui, an independent trade consultant. “Without a phased approach, the industry could see delays and reduced output.”

Government officials say they are monitoring the situation and remain in dialogue with industry leaders to address concerns. For now, the effects of the new tariff continue to ripple through factory floors and administrative offices across the country’s electrical equipment sector.
